title: Decide a repetition rule
why: Self-play games repeat exact positions often: 5.7% of big-board positions recur, mostly as four-ply cycles (repeat-points). The rules allow repetition, and the net has no history, so it cannot tell a cycle from progress. Random-stop ends the cycles played against a passing opponent (42% of big-board repeats); the rest, where both sides keep moving, run on to the cap. Options are in docs/history/GAMEPLAY_VARIANTS.md.
test: Find a position players would rationally repeat, then choose between unrestricted repetition, simple ko and superko.
revisit: If cycles where both sides keep moving still run to the cap in the 128 run; check the share of capped games with repeats.

title: Rebuild and check the Rust side after the Fedora upgrade
why: The upgrade moved system Python to 3.15 and broke training/.venv, which was rebuilt on a uv-managed 3.14. The Rust binaries were not rebuilt or run since.
test: cargo build --release, then correctness/check.sh.
result: Rebuilt in release mode on 2026-11-04; correctness/check.sh passed (Rust, 154 training and 33 dashboard tests).

title: Arena the value recipe, then adopt it
why: The value head memorized its window: train MAE 0.03, held-out 0.65. On update 23's 450k window, 16 labels per game cut held-out value MSE from 0.99 to 0.58 and lifted the winner from 71% to 79%. Policy KL fell as the value weight dropped and was flat at the no-value bound for weights of 1/8 and below. Stride-8 thinning plus weight decay already beat update 23 116-84. All held-out numbers are one seed.
test: Arena the 16-labels, weight-1/16 nets on update 23's window against update 23 and its twin on the 38 board, about 200 games. Two seeds. Then wire --value-labels-per-game 16 --value-weight 0.0625 and a 450k window into bulk-loop.sh.
result: Adopted: 172-28 (86%, about +315 Elo, 95% 0.81-0.91) for two seeds against update 23 and its twin, 43-7 in each of the four matches, pairs 73-1. bulk-loop.sh now trains --value-labels-per-game 16 --value-weight 0.0625 on a 450k window, 3 epochs, 5% turnover (VGO_ overrides for each).

title: Fix the rating pipeline
why: evaluation/ratings.py could not parse the loop's anchor records (its regex stops one level of nesting short of candidate_search.reuse), and the dashboard's strength curve anchors on sl-w64b16, which this run never plays. A fresh run would have no visible strength curve.
test: Parse anchor.jsonl from artifacts/vgo-bulk, anchor the curve on the run's own update 0, and show updates 3 to 29 on the dashboard with error bars.
result: evaluation/ratings.py parses nested records (27 matches, 162 games of this run now read). The dashboard anchors on the run's earliest update when the supervised baseline never played, so the strength curve shows. The rating prior drops from 2 virtual games to 0.1: at about 6 games a pairing the old prior halved the curve (update 8 +323 against +627). Rating rounds in bulk-loop.sh now play the 38 board at its 312-ply cap, and the reserved reference is the model 6 updates back instead of a fixed update 0, which leaves the pool once the run passes update 6. Cost: 18 big-board games every 3 updates, about 15-30 minutes of shared GPU, until random-stop shortens games.

title: Report value MSE or log loss, not MAE
why: MAE ranked an overconfident value head best: stride-8 thinning read 0.56 MAE but 0.70 MSE against 0.59 MSE for 16 labels per game. The learner's selection score and logs use MAE.
test: Add value MSE and cross-entropy to evaluate(), and use one of them in the selection score.
result: evaluate() reports value_mse and value_log_loss beside value_mae; epoch logs and the train/val line print MSE first. The diagnostic selection score is now policy_kl + value_mse at weight 1 (the final epoch is still what gets published). The dashboard's update rows carry value_mse.

title: End one-sided pass streaks at random, as a bootstrap
why: 72% of big-board games with a long pass streak ran to the 312-ply cap, so labels read who leads at ply 312. Once a side has passed 4 times running, ending the game with probability 0.25 on each further pass would have ended 74% of big-board games early, about 61 plies sooner, and changed the eventual winner in 13% of those. A stopgap until the value head supports hard resignation: no model input or search change, so it comes out cleanly.
test: Implement in self-play and arena only, seeded for reproducible digests. Check the share of capped games and plies per game in a short run.
result: RandomStop in vgo-selfplay's play_game, shared by self-play and the arena: --random-stop-after 4 --random-stop-probability 0.25, on by default in bulk-loop.sh for both generation and rating rounds. Seeded from the game seed and ply; game records carry random_stop, arena records random_stops, and SGFs a 'stopped' status. Off, games are unchanged: the four self-play digests match golden once the new random_stop field is removed from each record. A naive-play digest case now covers the stop. Not yet seen in a real run.

title: Find why stalling players repeat the same points
why: In recorded games the side behind alternated between the same two coordinates for about 150 plies. Your read: the move is a one-stone self-capture, so the board after it equals the board before, the net sees the same input, and it picks the same point again. Self-captures rose from 3% to 8-10% of plies over the run, which fits.
test: Replay the recorded positions: confirm the board is identical before and after each repeated move. If so, a move that leaves the board unchanged is a pass in disguise, which is a rule question for 5b4efdee.
result: Not board-unchanged moves: in self-play from update 12 on, only 0.4-0.8% of placements leave the board as it was, and none is answered by a pass. The stall is exact repetition: 5.7% of big-board positions (3.7% mid, 1.3% small) repeat an earlier position with the same side to move, almost all four plies apart, a two-move cycle where each move changes the board and the pair restores it. 42% of big-board repeats are one side cycling while the other passes, which random-stop ends; the other 58% are cycles where both sides move. The net cannot see a repetition: it has no history input.

title: Stop the naive generator once its window is full
why: The first update of a fresh run took 64 minutes against about 9, because the naive generator kept all 32 threads while training prepared batches, and it wrote 38 GB of games nobody trains on. Stopping it by hand brought the card straight back.
test: Touch the stop file when the first training starts, and confirm a fresh run's first update finishes in about 10 minutes.
result: bulk-loop.sh touches the naive generator's stop file when the first training starts. In a three-update scratch run, 8,026 of its 8,027 games predate the stop and the last finished in flight a second later. The same run confirmed random stops in self-play (55 of 332 model games) and rating rounds on 1/38 (about 255 plies a game).

title: Fresh overnight run with the fixes
why: Replaces forking from update 12: the fixes should help early phases too. Strength rose to about update 12 and then fell about 20 Elo an update, newer windows trained worse nets, and the value head memorized its window.
test: After value-recipe, random-stop, ratings-fix and naive-stop: start from the naive generator with the new recipe, and watch the rating curve for the rise-then-fall shape.
progress: Started 2026-11-04 in artifacts/vgo-128. Check 2026-11-05 17:30 at update 36 (~44 min/update): rose to ~+950 by update 24, then flat around +850-1050 to update 36 (6-game matches, +-150 each); no decline like the old run's. Value head still not memorizing (train MSE 0.756 vs held-out 0.763). Komi is lagging: Black's share went 59% -> 39%, and the 18-unit centre is falling 1 point a refit (the cap) toward even. Paused 2026-11-06 after update 47 for the warm-start test; flat from update 24 to 45 at about +800 (-2.6 Elo/update).

title: Fewer passes for value than for policy under warm start
why: In the warm chain, policy kept improving up to 8 passes per sample, but value memorized: the train/held-out MSE gap reached +0.18 and held-out value MSE rose from 0.735 (link 05) to 0.803 (link 09).
test: Offline chains like warm-2026-11-06 with (a) value labels per game 16 -> 4 on warm links, (b) value weight halved, (c) value head reinitialized each update. Compare held-out value MSE at link 09, then arena the best against the plain warm link 09.
progress: Watch the gap in the live loop's pt.json files first.

title: Warm-start training, capped at 8 passes per sample
why: The vgo-128 run has been flat from update 24 to 45 (-2.6 Elo/update, big board). Each update trains a fresh net on 450k samples, about 2,700 games, so nothing accumulates. The old warm-start loop lost 41-7 to from-scratch, but it made about 12 passes per sample (1 epoch on 150k every 12k). Held-out games are fixed per game (hash salted by shard digest), so a warm chain never trains on its validation games.
test: Offline: from update 38, 10 links of 1 epoch each on windows stepping 56k samples (12.5% turnover, so at most 8 passes per sample), ending on update 45's exact window. Compare with update 45 on held-out value MSE, policy KL and the train/held-out gap, then 40 games on 1/38. If it wins, run the loop with --initial-checkpoint, 1 epoch, turnover 0.125.
progress: 2026-11-06: the offline chain (update 38 -> 10 links, 1 epoch, 56k steps) beat from-scratch update 45 on its held-out games (policy KL 0.429 vs 0.457, top-1 13.7% vs 12.1%, value MSE 0.803 vs 0.815, sign 66.7% vs 64.7%) and won 31-9 on 1/38 (+215, roughly +100 to +390). Value overfits: train/held-out gap grew from ~0 to +0.18 and held-out value MSE rose after link 05. The loop now warm-starts (commit adf8c6b); resumed 2026-11-06 04:10 from update 48, generating with link-09 and warm-starting from it.

title: Let komi follow the result per board
why: Black's self-play win rate fell to about 10% on small boards and 30% on big ones, and the fitted fair komi was often below the sampler's floor. Partly a game-end effect, so decide after random-stop.
test: Measure Black's win rate by board after random-stop, then widen the range or fit the centre from recent games.
result: Built as dynamic recentring (training/loop/komi-calibration.py): refit before each generator, at most 1 point a refit, held until komi clearly moves the result; spread fixed at 5.46 points. The slope is logged for a later spread rule.

title: Train the faster net shapes
why: Fewer blocks, no attention and one norm take the card's ceiling at 128 from 21k positions/s to as much as 62k, but the generator stops gaining near 40k here. Trained nets read 30k for `blocks8` (no policy penalty in a loss screen), 35k for `c_d222_short_n1` (+0.013 KL) and 37k for `m_d111_c22` (+0.022 KL), against a seed spread of 0.003. Early in a run generation speed matters more than play, and any net's games train any shape, so a fast shape could generate first and the run could retrain to a stronger one later. Strength is unmeasured, and these rates need 15 to 20 vCPU per card: on 8 threads of 4 cores `blocks8` lost its whole gain within three minutes.
test: Arena `blocks8`, `c_d222_short_n1` and `m_d111_c22` against the current net at equal time on both boards, about 500 games each. Check a trained one over whole games on 8 vCPU. Checkpoints are in `artifacts/shape-screen/runs/`, and the dashboard's Net shapes tab shows the screen.
revisit: When choosing the net for the later, stronger phase of a run. m_d111_c22 already generates early.

title: Fixed-variance trunk: one norm per net instead of per block
why: KataGo's method has two halves. vgo already has the second: twin heads, the batch-normed set carrying 80% of the loss and the plain set used for inference. The first half, which vgo lacks, replaces every trunk norm with a fixed scale K, chosen so that idealized variance resets to 1, on pre-activation blocks. vgo's blocks are post-activation (relu after the add), so this is a block rewrite and a retrain. Speed: no trunk norms was +29% on the card for the old net, but the generator runs the GPU at ~71% at home and is CPU-bound on Vast, so throughput gains are small now. The real question is training quality.
test: Write the variance derivation for the DDRNet layout, where fusion sums two branches, and check activation variance at init. Then train control vs fixed-variance on one vgo-128 window and compare held-out KL; play an arena only if it ties or wins.
held: Needs the GPU and RAM the live run uses; the memory watchdog kills any train-once.py
revisit: When the vgo-128 run is paused or clearly plateaued

title: Nested bottleneck blocks for the stronger net
why: KataGo's block: 1x1 down to half width, two inner residual blocks of two 3x3s each, 1x1 up. Their b18c384 matched the old b40c256 on speed and came close to b60c320 on strength. vgo only has the plain bottleneck tail, with one 3x3, which KataGo found worse. It pays where full-width 3x3s dominate cost. In the current fast net (detail 1/1/1 at width 64) the fixed parts, norms and floor, take most of the time, and halving detail width alone cost +0.010 KL, so the gain is likely small now.
test: Add it as a shape in performance/model_variants.py, then time it and loss-screen it against a plain stack of equal cost at the wider/deeper size planned for the later phase.
held: Matters for the stronger net, not the fast generator net
revisit: With faster-net, when choosing the later-phase net

title: Cut the CPU work inside inference lanes
why: At 192 the lighter net reads 16.4k positions/s in the generator against a 23k card ceiling, with the CPU 60% idle. Each lane spends 28% of its time packing inputs and materializing outputs, about 1.1 ms a batch, and the card waits. A third lane makes it worse. Applying the board rotation twice per batch also wastes training CPU: the second call only needs the ownership map.
test: Time `input_packing` and `output_materialization` in broker telemetry before and after, then confirm in the generator.
revisit: Before renting: the home box is GPU-bound, but rented boxes have fewer CPUs per GPU.

title: Measure self-play on rented hardware
why: Here 8 vCPU hold 18.1k positions/s at 128 over whole games, at 95% GPU. A faster card needs more, about 5 vCPU per 10k positions/s by extrapolation, and rented hardware has different wake-up costs, so it needs checking on the real box.
test: Run 64 actors at 128 for 7 minutes pinned to half the cores, so games finish, and record positions/s, GPU use and busy cores.
revisit: Before renting hardware for a long run.

title: Decide the NumPy rasterizer
why: A hand-kept second rasterizer is a correctness risk if Rust covers every case.
test: Delete it unless something still needs the fallback.
revisit: Next time the training rasterizer is touched.

title: Spend search where it can change the result
why: Soft resignation is one narrow case of a general budget question: where does more search change the outcome, and where is it wasted? Framed that way, a yes-or-no concession becomes a search budget that follows how result-affecting the next moves are. There is no direct metric for this yet.
test: Record per-ply root value, KL(search policy || prior) and the value gap between the top two moves in a fresh run. See which of them predicts the result changing, then try a budget that follows it. info-metric is the first step. The dashboard's Reports tab has the ideas report.

title: Measure information per search directly
why: Nothing measures how much a search teaches. KL(search policy || prior) and value change per search would give a real signal-per-compute number.
test: Log both per position in a short run, and check they separate full searches from cheap ones.

title: Sweep the number of history steps
why: 3 plies of history cut held-out policy KL from 1.721 to 1.706 (top-1 0.122 to 0.127) with value unchanged, one seed, at 11 GB more training memory. Not needed yet. --history-plies exists in training; the Rust raster does not render the planes.
test: Train 1, 2, 3 and 4 plies on one window and compare held-out policy KL. If 1 ply carries most of it, render it in Rust and arena it.
revisit: After the fresh run is healthy.

title: Confirm 128 input as the efficient default
why: 128 searches 2-3.6x faster and scored 30-18 at equal time on the big board. One card plays 18.6k positions/s at 128, 7.4k at 192 and 4.1k at 256, so at 61 Elo a doubling 192 has to beat 128 by about 80 Elo at equal simulations and 256 by about 130.
test: Bootstrap at 128. Train a 192 net from scratch on the same window, then play them at equal time with --opponent-resolution on both boards. Move up once it wins.

title: Add a score head
why: Final scores have been recorded since 2026-09-24. Margin is richer than win or loss for each game.
test: Add after the ownership test, so the two effects can be told apart.

title: Add short-horizon value and opponent-move heads
why: Both can be labelled from existing games, adding more per-position signal.
test: Add one at a time, after ownership.

title: Branch from contested positions
why: sigmago's branch mining was never a fair test: 94% of roots were already decided, because it selected late positions.
test: Offline first: run several continuations from positions with values near even. Stop if they rarely disagree.

title: Revisit randomized search budgets
why: Gave 2.8x the games per hour, but 32 games were discarded and the pilot recipe was rejected. That doesn't rule out the idea.
test: Retry with a recipe that keeps a healthy policy target, judged at equal elapsed compute.

title: Rate models by game stage and board size
why: One rating hides regressions in the opening or endgame.
test: Extend arena records, and fit a rating per bucket.

title: Ablate the settled input plane
why: It's 92-96% of raster cost, and its strength benefit has never been measured.
test: Train with and without it on one corpus, then arena at equal time.

title: Tree reuse in self-play
why: Arena prototype scored 24-24 and 23-25, and inherited only 9-12 visits per hit.
test: No next step unless search budgets rise a lot.
